unit.title: Earth and Climate Change
unit.blurb: How convection currents move tectonic plates, the evidence that plates move, the carbon cycle, and the causes and effects of climate change.

O1.t: Explain how convection currents in the mantle move tectonic plates, and what happens at plate boundaries.

O2.t: Describe the evidence for tectonic plate movement.

O3.t: Describe the carbon cycle, including photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition and combustion.

O4.t: Describe the causes and impacts of climate change, past and present.

captions: Welcome to Camday.
This lesson was written by the Camday teaching team to
help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence.
Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 13: Earth and Climate Change.
Over millions of years, Earth's surface has changed as tectonic plates moved.
Today, the climate is changing in ways never seen before,
and rising seas are eating away coastlines.
A purple crystal of potassium manganate(VII) is placed at
the bottom of a large beaker of water,
at one side. The beaker is heated gently under that side only.
Predict: where will the purple colour go?
Pause and decide.
Watch. A purple stream rises straight up from the crystal, above the flame.
At the top it moves across,
sinks down the far side and flows back along the bottom: a loop.
Explain what you saw.
The heated water expands, becomes less dense and rises.
At the top it cools, becomes denser and sinks,
so the water moves round in a loop: a convection current.
Hot rock in Earth's mantle moves in the same way, very slowly,
carrying the tectonic plates with it.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
Earth's crust is made of huge rigid tectonic plates.
Below, in the mantle, hot magma rises, cools near the crust,
and sinks again: a convection current.
These currents drag the plates slowly along.
Where plates push together, rocks fold upwards into fold mountains.
Where they pull apart or slide under one another, volcanoes form.
And where they suddenly slip past each other, we get earthquakes.

p: A purple crystal sits at the bottom of a beaker of water, at one side. That side is heated gently.
p2: A purple stream rises above the flame, moves across the top, sinks down the far side and flows back along the bottom – a loop.
Heated water expands, becomes less dense and rises; at the top it cools, becomes denser and sinks: a **convection current**.

p: Earth's crust is broken into huge rigid **tectonic plates**. Below them, hot rock in the **mantle** moves very slowly in convection currents, dragging the plates along – a few centimetres a year.
Most mountains, volcanoes and earthquakes are found where plates meet.

head: Plates…

captions: For a long time, people didn't believe plates move.
One clue: the coasts of South America and Africa fit together like jigsaw pieces.
Scientists suggested there was once a single giant continent that broke apart.
Volcanoes and earthquakes occur mainly along plate boundaries,
such as the Pacific Ring of Fire, where plates are moving.
Identical fossils of Mesosaurus, a freshwater reptile,
are found in both South America and Africa.
It couldn't have swum across an ocean,
so the lands must once have been joined.
At the Mid-Atlantic Ridge,
rising magma cools into rock that records Earth's magnetic field,
which has flipped many times.
Matching stripes on both sides show the plates moving apart,
2.5 centimetres a year.

p: Look at a world map: the east coast of South America seems to fit into the west coast of Africa.
Is that just a coincidence?
In 1912 Alfred Wegener suggested that all the continents were once joined in one supercontinent, **Pangaea**, which slowly broke apart – **continental drift**.
p2: Many scientists rejected it at first because he could not explain **what** moved the continents. Later evidence – and the idea of mantle convection – showed he was right. Scientific ideas change as new evidence appears.

p: Four pieces of evidence:

head: Evidence
What it shows
rows: South America and Africa fit together like jigsaw pieces
fossils of the same freshwater reptile in South America and Africa – it could not have swum an ocean
they lie mainly along plate boundaries, such as the Pacific Ring of Fire
rocks on each side of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge record Earth's flipping magnetic field in matching stripes – the sea floor is spreading

p: Wegener proposed **continental drift** from a supercontinent, Pangaea.
Evidence: fitting coastlines, matching fossils, volcano and earthquake locations, magnetic stripes.
Ideas were accepted once evidence and a mechanism were found.

captions: Climate change is a change in Earth's long-term pattern of temperature,
wind and rainfall. In the past, asteroid impacts threw up dust that blocked sunlight,
and there were ice ages and even a 'snowball Earth'.
Records since 1880 show the planet is warming,
and the last 30 years have warmed much faster than the long-term rate.
Human activity is upsetting the carbon cycle.
Scientists predict more severe storms, droughts and floods.
Warmer oceans expand and ice sheets melt,
so sea levels rise about 3.5 millimetres a year,
threatening coastal cities like Jakarta.
NASA scientists compare each year's average global surface
temperature with the average for 1951 to 1980.
Before 1940 most years were cooler than that average.
Since 1980 every value shown is warmer.
By 2024, the warmest year on record,
the planet was 1.28 degrees Celsius above the 1951 to 1980 average.
Pause and decide: how has the rate of warming changed since 1980,
and what is the main cause?
Now it is your turn to shine!
Pause the video after each question and try to answer it first.
Question 1: What causes tectonic plates to move?
Pause the video now.
Answer: Convection currents in the mantle.
Question 2: Give two pieces of evidence for tectonic plates.
Pause the video now.
Answer: Fitting coastlines, matching fossils, volcano locations or magnetic stripes.
Question 3: Name two processes in the carbon cycle that release carbon dioxide.
Pause the video now.
Answer: Respiration and combustion (also decomposition).
Question 4: Why is sea level rising?
Pause the video now.
Answer: Warmer seawater expands and ice sheets melt.
